The Eurasian stone-curlew Burhinus oedicnemus exhibits a distinctive suite of life-history traits shaped by its semi-arid habitat. When incubated at the typical optimal temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the incubation period leading to hatching is approximately 25 days [ab = approximately 25 days]. Newly hatched chicks emerge at a wet weight of roughly 38.3 grams [Wwb = roughly 38.3 grams], a modest initial mass that reflects the semi-precocial developmental mode of this species, allowing the downy young to leave the nest and forage alongside their parents within hours of hatching. This early mobility is an advantage for a ground-nesting bird that relies on crypsis to avoid mammalian and avian predators. The rapid growth trajectory that follows is sustained by intensive biparental provisioning of invertebrates, with chicks gaining mass steadily throughout the nestling period. The energetic demands of the nestlings are considerable, as they must achieve sufficient body size and feather development to attain flight capability within a relatively compressed developmental window.

Under the thermal regime typical of an active adult at 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], the fledging period from hatching to first flight is 39 days [tx = 39 days]. This milestone marks the transition to nutritional independence, though juveniles often remain in proximity to the natal territory for several subsequent weeks while refining foraging skills. The attainment of flight is a critical juncture in the life cycle, as it greatly enhances escape from ground-based predators and expands the chick's access to foraging patches. Available data indicate that the age at puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation, occurs at 117 days after hatching [tp = 117 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This relatively early maturation, compared to many other Charadriiformes of similar body size, allows young birds to integrate into the adult breeding population in their first spring. However, successful reproduction in the first year is contingent upon territory establishment and the acquisition of a mate, both of which can be limited by habitat saturation.

The reproductive output of this species is modest but consistent, reflecting the constraints of nesting in open environments where clutch predation rates can be high. Females typically lay two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], a clutch size that balances the energetic investment in each large, cryptically patterned egg against the probability of total brood loss. Under the thermal conditions of adult life at 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is achieved when females produce one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], a frequency that is typical of temperate populations with a sufficiently long breeding season. This rate of reproduction is relatively low for a bird of its body size, consistent with a slower life-history pace that prioritizes adult survival in an unpredictable environment. Replacement clutches are commonly laid if the initial attempt fails, extending the reproductive effort into the summer months. The two-egg clutch appears to be evolutionarily conserved across the Burhinus genus.

Adult females of the Eurasian stone-curlew attain an ultimate wet weight of 535.2 grams [Wwi = 535.2 grams], placing them among the larger-bodied members of the family Burhinidae. Field records indicate that individual body mass can vary from 290 to 535 grams (290-535 grams) [Wwi = 290-535 grams], likely reflecting seasonal fluctuations in fat deposition associated with migratory preparation or winter resource scarcity. This pronounced mass range underscores the importance of body condition for surviving lean periods. The substantial size dimorphism is minimal in this species, though females tend toward the upper end of the range during the pre-laying period when they carry developing eggs. Adult body mass is closely tied to foraging success on agricultural land and fallow fields, where the birds feed nocturnally on insects, mollusks, and small vertebrates. The energetic demands of maintaining this body mass are met through a highly visual, stop-and-wait foraging strategy well suited to detecting prey in low-light conditions.

The maximum recorded lifespan of the Eurasian stone-curlew in the wild is estimated at 17.9 years [am = 17.9 years], a considerable longevity for a wader of this mass and one that underscores the species' low annual adult mortality once territory ownership is established at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. Under the metabolic framework typical of adult birds at 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], the time since birth at first brood is 730 days [tR = 730 days], meaning that most individuals do not successfully breed until their second calendar year. This delay is consistent with the need to secure a stable breeding territory, which often requires prospecting and contesting with established residents during the first year. The long lifespan allows multiple reproductive attempts over an individual's life, offsetting the relatively low annual fecundity. Senescence-related declines in reproductive output have not been documented in this species, but the oldest breeding birds likely experience decreasing foraging efficiency and an accompanying reduction in chick provisioning rates.
